The red bigeye, Priacanthus macracanthus, is a moderately sized tropical priacanthid that supports artisanal fisheries throughout the Indo-West Pacific. Field studies conducted on the continental shelf off northeastern Taiwan indicate that this species reaches a maximum fork length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm], a value that places it among the larger members of its genus. The size at which individuals first attain sexual maturity is considerably smaller, with a fork length at puberty of 18.9 cm [Lp = 18.9 cm] recorded from gonadal inspection of over 600 specimens. This size corresponds to an estimated wet weight at puberty of 101 grams [Wwp = 101 grams], a threshold that is typically reached during the second year of life under prevailing thermal regimes. In fully grown reproductively active adults, the gonadosomatic index (GSI) reaches a maximum average value of 7% [GSI = 7%] at a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], coinciding with the peak of the summer spawning season.

The egg diameter of Priacanthus macracanthus has been measured at 0.52 mm from freshly spawned, water-hardened oocytes collected during plankton tows. Using the standard geometric formula for a sphere, this diameter yields an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.000074 grams [Wwb = 0.000074 grams] per fertilized ovum. This minute neonatal mass is typical of pelagic-spawning teleosts that produce numerous, small, yolk-poor eggs and rely on a protracted larval phase in the water column. Upon hatching, the yolk-sac larva emerges at an endotrophic stage and depends entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves until the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding commences, a trophic switch that generally occurs within two to three days after eclosion at ambient tropical temperatures. The small size of the newly hatched larva imposes tight constraints on the size of its initial prey, typically requiring rotifers or small copepod nauplii as a first food source in the wild.

The growth trajectory of Priacanthus macracanthus from settlement to adulthood is well described by a power function fitted to fork length and body mass data from fishery-independent surveys. Using the length–weight relationship derived for the species, the asymptotic or ultimate wet weight of a fish reaching the maximum fork length of 30 cm is estimated at 413 grams [Wwi = 413 grams]. This value corresponds to a robust, fully grown adult that has completed its somatic development and is capable of sustaining repeated spawning events over several seasons. When maintained at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for this species in mark-recapture studies is 10 years [am = 10 years], a longevity that is consistent with its moderate size and relatively slow growth rate after maturity. By contrast, smaller congeners in the genus often exhibit shorter maximum longevities, suggesting that body size is a key determinant of lifespan within the Priacanthidae.

Sexual maturation in male Priacanthus macracanthus is accompanied by a marked increase in testicular mass and the onset of active spermatogenesis, while females undergo vitellogenesis that culminates in the production of several batches of pelagic eggs per spawning season. The transition to the reproductively active state occurs at a fork length of 18.9 cm [Lp = 18.9 cm], a criterion that was confirmed through histological examination of gonadal tissue across a wide size range of individuals. Individuals below this fork length were uniformly immature, with no evidence of prior spawning activity, whereas all specimens exceeding 20 cm fork length showed clear signs of active or recent gametogenesis. Gonadal inspection of over 600 specimens revealed that puberty is attained at a body mass of approximately 101 grams [Wwp = approximately 101 grams], a threshold typically reached during the second year of life. Although capable of spawning at this mass, first reproduction may be deferred if environmental conditions are unfavorable.

At a sustained temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the gonadosomatic index attains its peak value of 7% [GSI = 7%] during the height of the reproductive period. This elevated GSI coincides with the seasonal peak in phytoplankton and zooplankton abundance, ensuring that the resulting ichthyoplankton has access to adequate prey during the critical early feeding stages. The maximum fork length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm] represents the upper limit of asymptotic size in this population; individuals approaching this length are typically more than a decade old, as the species exhibits diminishing growth increments after puberty. The oldest individual documented in the mark-recapture dataset lived for ten years [am = ten years], a period that encompasses numerous spawning seasons and underscores the iteroparous, batch-spawning life history that characterizes Priacanthus macracanthus across its geographic rang at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]e.
